records.sourceFile: Personalized resistance training mitigates neuromuscular and perceived fatigue - The autoregulation cluster training method.pdf

paper.citation: Dello Iacono A, Hillan J, Watson K. Personalizing Resistance Training Mitigates Neuromuscular and Perceived Fatigue: The Autoregulation Cluster Training Method. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2023. Ahead of print.
paper.abstract: Twenty-six resistance-trained men completed bench press and back squat sessions at 75% 1RM, matched for load, volume (24 repetitions) and total rest (240 s), using traditional sets (3 x 8 with 120 s rest), interset rest redistribution (6 x 4 with 48 s between clusters) and autoregulation cluster training (ACT), in which the cluster structure was adjusted during the session to a 20% velocity loss target. IRR and ACT produced less velocity loss than TRA, and ACT produced less velocity loss and rate of fatigue than IRR. The authors conclude that cluster structures reduced neuromuscular and perceived fatigue and that ACT was the most effective.
paper.tldr: In resistance-trained men, cluster-set structures reduced within-session velocity loss and perceived fatigue compared with traditional sets at the same load, volume and total rest. An autoregulated cluster method reduced both more than a fixed cluster structure, but this was a single-session study.
paper.methods: Randomized crossover design with 26 resistance-trained men (mean age 26.7 years). Each man completed three sessions in randomized order (TRA, IRR, ACT) with bench press and back squat at 75% 1RM, 24 repetitions and 240 s total rest, separated by 48 to 72 hours. Mean propulsive velocity was measured with a linear encoder and rate of fatigue was rated on an 11-point scale (0 to 10) within 5 minutes of each exercise. Linear mixed-effects models tested training structure and exercise.
paper.findings: Velocity loss was lower for IRR and ACT pooled than TRA (b = -2.09, P < .001) and lower for ACT than IRR (b = -2.31, P < .001), with no significant structure by exercise interaction; the back squat had greater velocity loss than the bench press (b = 1.83, P < .001). Mean velocity loss was 19.8%, 15.9% and 11.3% for bench press (TRA, IRR, ACT) and 23.3%, 16.6% and 12.6% for back squat (Table 2). Rate of fatigue was lower for IRR and ACT than TRA (b = -0.64, P < .001) and for ACT than IRR (b = -1.05, P < .001). In ACT, 87% of bench press and 82% of back squat repetitions were within the 20% velocity loss target.
paper.limitations: Only men were studied, with two exercises, one load (75% 1RM) and one comparator cluster structure. Lactate and other metabolic markers were not measured, so the mechanisms are speculative. Dello Iacono and Watson declare a conflict of interest as part of the team that developed the ACT mobile app. The Results text prints the pooled IRR and ACT vs TRA velocity loss contrast as b = 2.09, but the abstract, Table 3 and the printed 95% CI (-2.46 to -1.72) all give -2.09, so the text sign is a typo. The first Results paragraph is labelled as rate of fatigue but reports the velocity loss interaction values from Table 3 (b = -0.81 and 0.34, not significant). Outcomes are acute, within-session measures only.
paper.practicalImplications: ACT is a reasonable option for personalized cluster-set prescription in resistance-trained men when the goal is to limit within-session velocity loss and perceived fatigue. It requires velocity measurement during the session, which many staff will not have. Total rest and volume were matched across conditions, so ACT did not add training time in this study.
paper.athleteDev: Within a session, cluster-set structures reduced velocity loss and perceived fatigue compared with traditional sets at matched load, volume and total rest, and the autoregulated version reduced both most. Use this to manage within-session fatigue. The study does not show gains in strength, power or sport performance.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The sample was healthy, resistance-trained men and no injured or rehabilitating participants were studied, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Physiological Resilience - What Is It and How Might It Be Trained.pdf

paper.citation: Jones AM, Kirby BS. Physiological Resilience: What Is It and How Might It Be Trained? Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2025;35(3):e70032.
paper.abstract: Physiological resilience is proposed as an additional factor in endurance performance, reflecting how VO2max, efficiency and metabolic thresholds deteriorate during prolonged exercise. The authors describe the physiological basis, practical testing approaches, and the available evidence on training. They suggest that long-term training consistency and volume, prolonged sessions including high-intensity or progressive efforts, and heavy strength and plyometric training may enhance resilience, while noting that the data are scant.
paper.tldr: Physiological resilience (how well VO2max, economy and thresholds hold up during prolonged exercise) may be a separate determinant of endurance performance. Evidence on training is limited, so long-term volume, prolonged sessions with race-pace or progressive efforts, and heavy strength and plyometric work are candidates to test rather than established methods.
paper.methods: Narrative review and perspective by two authors. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or appraisal method is described. The review draws on the Joyner model, data from Clark et al. (critical power after 2 hours of heavy cycling, 36 participants pooled from three studies), and observational and small training studies, including one unpublished doctoral thesis.
paper.findings: After 2 hours of heavy-intensity cycling, critical power fell by about 10% at group mean, with individual declines from 1% to 33%, and the decline was not explained by baseline VO2max or fresh critical power. Substrate shifts toward fat accounted for about 30% of the rise in VO2 over that period. Unhjem reported smaller increases in O2 cost in trained runners than in active adults. Zanini et al. (ref 44) reported a 2.4% change in O2 cost in the higher-performing group versus 4.5% in the lower group. Heavy strength training improved performance after prolonged exercise in cyclists (Ronnestad et al.) and in cross-country skiers (Ofsteng et al.). The authors state that no longitudinal study has targeted training for resilience.
paper.limitations: Narrative review with no described search or appraisal method. The Clark studies used non-elite participants, and the authors caution about extrapolation to highly trained athletes. The Figure 1 model adds a generic resilience factor based on another dataset, so its accuracy gain is illustrative. Several training claims rest on an unpublished thesis (ref 59) and on speculation about super-shoe effects, which the authors label as tempting but untested. One author is affiliated with the Nike Sport Research Lab, and the paper declares no conflicts of interest.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches of endurance athletes can consider long-term training consistency and volume, some race-pace or progressive long sessions, and regular heavy strength and plyometric work as candidates for building resilience. These are hypotheses rather than validated methods, so staff could track fatigued-state performance or economy to see whether a programme is working. Added training should be balanced against recovery, because the authors note the risk of overreaching.
paper.athleteDev: Resilience, the decline in fresh-state capacities during long efforts, may matter for endurance performance. Long-term consistent volume, race-pace and progressive long sessions, and heavy strength and plyometric training are plausible ways to build it, but none has been tested for resilience directly. Fatigued-state testing of athletes could show whether a programme is working.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The review covers performance physiology in endurance athletes and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Physiological adaptations and practical efficacy of different blood flow restriction resistance training modes in athletic populations.pdf

paper.citation: He C, Zhu D, Hu Y. Physiological adaptations and practical efficacy of different blood flow restriction resistance training modes in athletic populations. Frontiers in Physiology. 2025;16:1683442.
paper.abstract: This review compares three blood flow restriction resistance training (BFRT) modalities in athletes: low-load training with BFR (BFR-LIRT), high-load training supplemented with BFR (S-BFRRT), and periodized combined high-load and BFR training (C-BFRRT). It links each modality to a proposed mechanism and training phase, and it offers a framework for rehabilitation, competitive and preparatory periods. The authors describe the framework as preliminary rather than a definitive prescription.
paper.tldr: Blood flow restriction training comes in three forms for athletes, and the review links each to a different mechanism and training phase. These links are the authors' proposed framework, drawn from 14 small studies, and are not validated prescriptions.
paper.methods: The authors searched CNKI, PubMed and Web of Science, identified 412 articles, and included 14 studies of athletes with structured BFRT and control groups; they also state that Table 1 was selected to give a representative overview rather than an exhaustive systematic inventory. Table 1 summarizes the included studies by modality, sport, load, pressure, duration and outcome. Table 2 gives programming ranges that the authors state come from a qualitative synthesis of targeted database searches and should be read as practical guidelines rather than unequivocal prescriptions.
paper.findings: For BFR-LIRT at 20 to 30% 1RM, the text states that Korkmaz et al. (n = 23 football players, 6 weeks) found greater rectus femoris thickness and knee strength gains than high-load training (p < 0.05), but Table 1 marks only the rectus femoris change as better than the control group and the strength change as within-group only. The review cites a meta-analysis reporting moderate strength gains (effect size 0.65) for BFR-LIRT, although the reference title describes BFR combined with high-load training, and it notes two studies with weaker or null results. For C-BFRRT, small studies (Che et al. 2022, n = 16; Sarfabadi et al. 2023, n = 16; Zhu 2021, n = 20) reported gains superior to conventional training, while for S-BFRRT the text reports that Scott et al. 2017 found no added benefit in preseason; the review gives no pooled estimates comparing modalities.
paper.limitations: The authors call this a narrative review, and the included studies are small (6 to 32 athletes) with varied pressures, durations and outcomes. Table 1 conflicts with the text for Korkmaz et al. 2022 (table: strength change within-group only; text: strength gains surpassing high-load training), Scott et al. 2017 (table: superior to HLRT over 6 weeks; text: no added benefit over 5 weeks) and Yamanaka et al. 2012 (table: rectus femoris CSA increased; text: no limb hypertrophy). The review also gives no statistical detail for most comparisons and states that the most effective load range is 20 to 50% 1RM without a citation.
paper.practicalImplications: Within this review's framework, BFR-LIRT at 20 to 30% 1RM may suit rehabilitation and in-season maintenance, and combined periodized BFR may suit hypertrophy blocks, but the authors present these as proposals. The proposed phase plan (8 to 12 weeks of preparation, 4 to 6 weeks of competition, 2 to 4 weeks of transition) and the pressure and duration ranges in Table 2 should not be treated as established protocols. The review notes that thrombosis risk and long-term safety are under-studied, and it recommends keeping total occlusion within the 15 to 30 minute range it describes.
paper.athleteDev: The review proposes BFR-LIRT for strength maintenance and tissue-sparing hypertrophy, S-BFRRT for concurrent strength and hypertrophy in competitive phases, and C-BFRRT for hypertrophy in preparation phases. This phase plan rests on small studies and the authors' hypotheses, and the review does not test it against sport performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The review suggests BFR-LIRT may support rehabilitation after injury, but its examples come from case-level reports, including a two-decathlete case report on patellar tendinopathy (Cuddeford and Brumitt, 2020) per the reference title. It gives no return-to-play criteria, so it cannot be used to set return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Planned Load Reduction Versus Fixed Load- A Strategy to Reduce the Perception of Effort With Similar Improvements in Hypertrophy and Strength.pdf

paper.citation: Lima BM, Amancio RS, Gonçalves DS, Koch AJ, Curty VM, Machado M. Planned load reduction versus fixed load: a strategy to reduce the perception of effort with similar improvements in hypertrophy and strength. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018;13(9):1164-1168.
paper.abstract: Twenty-one recreationally resistance-trained men were randomized to constant 10RM load (CON), 5% load reduction after each set (RED 5) or 10% load reduction after each set (RED 10) during 16 weeks of biceps and Scott curl training, with each set taken to volitional fatigue. Muscle thickness and 10RM increased in all groups with no between-group differences, and volume load did not differ. RED 10 gave a lower average daily RPE than CON for the biceps curl and than CON and RED 5 for the Scott curl.
paper.tldr: In recreationally trained men, a 10% load reduction across sets gave muscle and strength gains similar to constant-load training while lowering perceived effort. The study used two elbow flexor exercises with 7 men per group, so it does not show whether the effect holds for multijoint lifts.
paper.methods: Three groups (CON, RED 5, RED 10; n = 7 each) trained 3 days per week for 16 weeks, performing 3 sets of biceps and Scott curls to volitional fatigue with 1 minute of rest between sets. Muscle thickness of the elbow flexors was measured by B-mode ultrasound before and after training, and 10RM was retested every 2 weeks from week 2 to week 14. Volume load and average daily RPE were calculated for each condition and compared between groups by one-way ANOVA.
paper.findings: Muscle thickness increased in all groups (P < .001) with no group x time difference (P = .976). The 10RM biceps curl and Scott curl increased in all groups (P < .001) with no between-group differences (Scott curl P = .238; biceps curl P = .401). Volume load did not differ between groups (biceps curl P = .649; Scott curl P = .094). Average daily RPE was lower for RED 10 than CON for the biceps curl (6.8 [0.3] vs 7.3 [0.9]; overall P = .002) and, for the Scott curl, lower for RED 10 than CON (6.8 [0.1] vs 7.0 [0.1]; P < .001) and RED 5 (7.1 [0.1]; P = .001). Pooled correlations between biceps-curl volume load and change in biceps curl 10RM were modest and negative (r = -.522, P = .015).
paper.limitations: Only 7 men per group, two single-joint elbow flexor exercises and 3 sets per exercise. The authors suggest total volume may have been too low to detect hypertrophy differences. The RPE differences were 0.2 to 0.5 points, and the correlations pool all groups, so they are not group comparisons. Multijoint lifts were not tested, as the authors note. The abstract reports the Scott-curl volume values as total volume and gives P = .001 for the biceps-curl RPE difference, whereas the results give P = .002 for the overall biceps-curl RPE test; the results values are used here.
paper.practicalImplications: In this 16-week elbow flexor program, a 10% load reduction after each set did not change total volume, muscle thickness or 10RM compared with constant load, but it lowered perceived effort. Staff should use it as a way to reduce effort during training, not as a method to add volume or extra gains, and it has not been tested on squats or other multijoint lifts.
paper.athleteDev: In recreationally trained men doing biceps and Scott curls, a 10% load reduction after each set produced hypertrophy and strength gains similar to constant load while lowering perceived effort. The study did not include athletes or multijoint exercises, so transfer to those settings is untested.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It enrolled healthy recreationally trained men with no injured participants and tested no rehabilitation outcome.

records.sourceFile: Player-Level Tackle Training Interventions in Tackle-Collision Sports - A Systematic Scoping Review.pdf

paper.citation: Davidow D, Paul L, Jones B, Hohlfeld A, Rasenyalo S, Dane K, et al. Player-level tackle training interventions in tackle-collision sports: a systematic scoping review. Sports Med Open. 2025;11:103.
paper.abstract: A systematic scoping review (PRISMA-ScR, four databases to May 2024) of 13 studies that tested player-level tackle training in American football and rugby, with 503 athletes in total. The authors report that all interventions produced favorable changes in their outcome measures, which were mainly tackle technique, kinematics and head impact measures.
paper.tldr: Player-level tackle training has a small, mostly short-term evidence base in American football and rugby. Two randomized trials of helmetless tackle training reported fewer head impacts than controls, but no included study reported injury incidence as an outcome.
paper.methods: The authors followed the Arksey and O'Malley scoping review framework with Levac et al. refinements and PRISMA-ScR, and registered the protocol with OSF. PubMed, EBSCOhost, Web of Science and Scopus were searched from January 2000 to 30 May 2024, two reviewers screened records, and one reviewer charted the data with corroboration by a second. Study quality was rated with JBI checklists for quasi-experimental studies and randomized trials, and no study was excluded on quality.
paper.findings: Of 5,656 records, 13 full-text studies met the criteria: seven in American football (360 athletes), and six in rugby union and rugby league (143 athletes), with eight studies including only males. Interventions were mostly tackler-focused instruction or feedback delivered by video or expert coach, plus an 8-week strength and power program, helmetless training, and data-informed practice design. In the two randomized trials of helmetless training, the authors report 30% fewer head impacts per athlete exposure than controls in college players (Swartz 2015, n=50) and 26% to 33% fewer game-related head impacts in youth players (Swartz 2019, n=180).
paper.limitations: Because this is a scoping review, the authors did not pool or grade effects. The abstract calls study quality 'good', but the results report only JBI checklist scores with no stated cutoff for 'good' (quasi-experimental studies averaged 7 of 9, range 4 to 9; the two randomized trials scored 10 and 11 of 13). Most studies were small, short-term and in youth or amateur players, one was a single-player case study and another had three participants, and outcomes were technique, kinematics or head impacts rather than injury incidence, which the authors list as a need for future studies.
paper.practicalImplications: When planning tackle training, staff can use video feedback combined with expert instruction and standardized technique criteria, which the authors recommend based on the included studies. The review does not establish which program reduces match concussion or injury risk, so these methods should be monitored in the team's own technique and head-impact data rather than presented as proven injury prevention.
paper.athleteDev: Video feedback with instruction and standardized scoring improved tackle technique or proficiency scores in several small studies in youth, amateur and college players. The review does not show that these methods improve performance at higher levels of play.
paper.rtp: Not applicable: the review contains no injured-player samples and no return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Positional differences in muscle to bone ratio in National Football League players.pdf

paper.citation: Dengel DR, Evanoff N. Positional Differences in Muscle-to-Bone Ratio in National Football League Players. International Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023.
paper.abstract: DXA scans of 346 NFL players were compared with 228 age-matched healthy male controls to examine total and regional muscle-to-bone ratio (lean mass divided by bone mineral content), and the ratio was compared across positions.
paper.tldr: NFL players had a slightly lower total muscle-to-bone ratio than controls despite more lean mass and bone, and the total ratio did not differ by position. Leg ratio did vary by position, but its link to performance or injury was not studied.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of whole-body and regional DXA scans (GE Lunar iDXA, enCore 16.2) from 2006 to 2011. Muscle-to-bone ratio was lean mass divided by bone mineral content; group comparisons used t-tests and position comparisons used ANOVA with Tukey HSD.
paper.findings: NFL players had a lower total (18.50 vs 19.12, P < .001) and trunk muscle-to-bone ratio than controls, a higher arm ratio (17.70 vs 16.48, P < .0001), and no difference in leg ratio (16.72 vs 16.85, P = .34). The total ratio did not differ across positions. Leg ratio was lowest in punters and kickers (15.7) and quarterbacks (15.8) and highest in offensive linemen (17.9) and defensive linemen (17.7).
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional and retrospective (2006-2011 data), and controls were drawn from population studies rather than athletes. The abstract describes NFL players' percent body fat as 'significantly lower' than controls, but the reported P = .053 is not significant at .05. The Methods state paired t-tests for two independent groups, and the authors' explanation of the lower total ratio (greater height and skeleton size) was not tested; no performance or injury outcomes are included.
paper.practicalImplications: A DXA scan gives total and regional lean mass and bone values that staff could use for body composition profiling, but the paper reports position averages only and gives no thresholds for individual decisions. Staff should not read a player's ratio against these averages as a bone-health or performance marker without outcome data.
paper.athleteDev: Leg muscle-to-bone ratio varied by position, which may describe position-specific body composition, but the paper does not link it to speed, strength or game performance.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return to sport. The study has no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Positional movement demands during NFL football games - A 3-year review.pdf

paper.citation: Sanchez E, Weiss L, Williams T, Ward P, Peterson B, Wellman A, et al. Positional Movement Demands during NFL Football Games: A 3-Year Review. Applied Sciences. 2023;13:9278.
paper.abstract: Player tracking data from 768 NFL regular-season games (2018-2020) were used to quantify on-field distance, maximum velocity, high-velocity efforts, and acceleration and deceleration efforts by position, using position-specific velocity thresholds.
paper.tldr: Game movement demands differ clearly by position: receivers and defensive backs cover the most distance and reach the highest speeds, receivers make the most accelerations, and linemen have the lowest totals on every load measure. These averages can serve as position benchmarks, but they describe games and not injury risk.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of Next Gen Stats tracking (10 Hz) during on-field play from kickoff to the end of each game, summarized per player-game. High-velocity efforts used 85% of each position's 75th-percentile maximum velocity; acceleration and deceleration efforts used 3.5 m/s^2. One-way ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests compared positions.
paper.findings: In-game maximum velocity was highest for cornerbacks (31.4 km/h), safeties (30.8 km/h) and receivers (30.7 km/h) and lowest for offensive linemen (20.4 km/h). Linebackers had the most high-velocity efforts (5.1 per game) and distance (98.5 m), and offensive linemen the fewest (1.4 efforts). Receivers had the most acceleration efforts (65.7 per game) and safeties the most deceleration efforts (23.5 per game); nearly all between-position differences were significant.
paper.limitations: Only on-field tracking was used, with no collision data, injury or performance outcomes; the authors note that blocking and tackling are not captured. The Discussion says safeties had the most acceleration efforts on defense with linebackers close behind, but Table 2 gives cornerbacks 42.3, linebackers 41.1 and safeties 40.4; the abstract's statement that receivers and defensive backs had more acceleration efforts than other positions also conflicts with Table 2, where tight ends (49.6) exceed both defensive back groups. Table 2 values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: Position averages and the 85%-of-positional-maximum thresholds can help performance staff benchmark practice and preseason targets for each group, especially for sprint, acceleration and deceleration volume. The authors also suggest the data may help plan return-to-play loads, but this study did not test that use.
paper.athleteDev: Gives position-level benchmarks for in-game sprint, acceleration and deceleration volume that can guide training design. The authors state that run and pass plays should be analyzed separately before firm conclusions are drawn.
paper.rtp: Can give game-demand context for return-to-play planning, but the study does not measure injury, rehabilitation progress or readiness, so it cannot set return criteria. The authors' suggestion that it may help return-to-play protocols is untested here.

records.sourceFile: Preseason and in-season high speed running demands of 2 professional Australian Rules football teams.pdf

paper.citation: Freeman BW, Talpey SW, James LP, Rayner RJ, Young WB. Preseason and In-Season High-Speed Running Demands of 2 Professional Australian Rules Football Teams. Sports Health. 2024.
paper.abstract: GPS data from 55 male athletes at two professional Australian Rules football clubs were used to compare high-speed running volume in the 2019 preseason and the first eight in-season rounds. Weekly running in the 71 to 80% and 81 to 90% Vmax bands was greater in preseason, with large individual variation in distance at each speed band.
paper.tldr: Preseason high-speed running volume in professional Australian Rules football was higher than in the early season for mid-to-high speed bands. Individual exposure varied widely, so team averages hide athletes with very low sprint exposure.
paper.methods: Observational cohort study using Catapult GPS data (10 Hz) from training and matches. Individual Vmax came from the first four preseason weeks and was updated if higher. Weekly distance in absolute and relative speed bands was compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and individual variation was summarized as coefficients of variation.
paper.findings: Weekly distance in the 71 to 80% Vmax band (P < 0.01, r = 0.56) and 81 to 90% Vmax band (P < 0.01, r = 0.58) was greater in preseason than in-season; the 91 to 100% Vmax band did not differ significantly (P = 0.10, r = 0.22). Club A differed in all three bands, but Club B differed only in the 71 to 80% band. Mean weekly total distance was 30,967 m in preseason and 29,909 m in-season, and 6 athletes did not reach 95% Vmax in preseason.
paper.limitations: Two clubs, one season, and a sample of 55 athletes limit generalizability. No injury or performance outcomes were analyzed, and the authors state that the link between this volume and injury risk is unknown. The abstract labels the bands as above 70% and above 80% Vmax with P = 0.01, while the Results report the 71 to 80% and 81 to 90% Vmax bands with P < 0.01, and the Discussion states that all three bands were significantly lower in-season although the Results report P = 0.103 for 91 to 100% Vmax. Weekly values were calculated as the summed session distance divided by the number of sessions that week, so they are per-session averages rather than weekly totals.
paper.practicalImplications: Review individual speed-band exposure rather than team averages when planning preseason and early-season running, because some athletes covered very little distance above 90% Vmax. Track each athlete's maximum speed through the season, since 36 athletes recorded a higher Vmax in the first eight rounds than in preseason. The study does not establish a dose that reduces injury.
paper.athleteDev: The study describes preseason and in-season high-speed running volume and shows that it varies widely between athletes. It does not show that any running dose improves performance.
paper.rtp: The study does not include injured athletes or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot guide return-to-play running progressions or clearance. It does not establish a sprint dose that prevents soft-tissue injury.

records.sourceFile: Programing high-speed and sprint running exposure in football - Beliefs and practices of more than 100 practitioners worldwide.pdf

paper.citation: Dello Iacono A, Beato M, Unnithan VB, Shushan T. Programming high-speed and sprint running exposure in football: beliefs and practices of more than 100 practitioners worldwide. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2023 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: An online survey of 102 football practitioners from 22 countries asked about the importance, timing, monitoring, training methods and perceived effectiveness of high-speed and sprint running exposure. Respondents agreed on importance, scheduled exposure differently for starting and nonstarting players, and lacked consensus on how to define and monitor these metrics.
paper.tldr: A survey of 102 football practitioners found broad agreement that high-speed and sprint running exposure matters, but wide variation in how it is defined, monitored and scheduled. Respondent beliefs do not establish which practices work.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional online survey (Qualtrics) of football practitioners recruited by convenience sampling, covering five domains: who, why, when, what and how, with data collected March 9 to July 5, 2022. Analyses used descriptive statistics, a mixed-effects logistic model for exposure timing by player status, and multinomial logistic models for match-outcome targets.
paper.findings: Practitioners agreed that exposure is important for physical development, competition preparation and injury prevention. Most ranked official matches as the greatest exposure for starting players and complementary training for nonstarters, and the authors report that nonstarters' odds of training-based exposure were 2.74 times those of starters (95% CI 2.09 to 3.72). Using a 100% match-outcome target, predicted probabilities were 33%, 48% and 19% for single, two-microdose and multiple-microdose HSR strategies, but the match-outcome odds ratios were not significant (p = .108 and .227 for HSR). Conditioning and drill-based training were rated most effective, while game-based formats were rated at least moderately effective.
paper.limitations: The sample is a convenience sample dominated by Italian and male respondents, and players' level and sex were not fully represented, so the results may not reflect other clubs or leagues. Table 3 is hard to interpret because it is labelled by exposure timing while the text describes player status, so the 2.74 odds ratio should be checked against the table. The authors acknowledge the evidence base is level 5 and that the match-outcome predictions are uncertain.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could use the finding that starters and nonstarters are exposed to sprinting at different times as a prompt to plan separate compensatory sessions for nonstarters. The authors' suggestion of two sessions roughly 48 hours apart between MD+2 and MD-2 is a practical option for them to test, not a tested standard.
paper.athleteDev: The paper addresses how practitioners plan high-speed and sprint running exposure within the microcycle, including scheduling and the use of microdosed sessions. It does not measure physical adaptation, performance or injury outcomes, so it cannot show that any scheduling choice improves development.
paper.rtp: The paper does not address return to sport, rehabilitation or injury recovery, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. Its injury-prevention comments are the practitioners' views, not measured outcomes.
